title: I cut my self-portrait into 24,236 pieces. Here's the economics behind it.
excerpt: Why does the first piece cost $77 and the last one $777? An honest text about art, capitalism, manufactured scarcity — and why I'm laying the math bare.
content:
I painted my self-portrait in oil. Then I cut it up — on paper, into 24,236 identical rectangles. Each rectangle gets a number, a certificate, and its own price. The more pieces sold, the more expensive the next one becomes. No marketing gimmick. That is the project. This text explains why — the honest way, not the way galleries usually talk.

I'm Simon, born in Germany, living in Switzerland. On i-laugh-you.com I sell numbered fragments of this one oil painting. The first piece costs $77. The last one will cost $777. Between them, a curve bends upward — the emptier the canvas, the more expensive what's left.

The math behind the price (no formula)

Concretely: 24,236 pieces. Piece number 1 costs $77. Piece 12,118, the mathematical midpoint, sits at around $200. Piece number 24,236 costs exactly $777. Every single piece in between is a tiny bit more expensive than the previous one. At the start you barely notice. Toward the end the curve gets steep.

The rise is exponential, not linear. Not because I'm greedy, but because that's how the world works. Whoever buys early pays for the belief that this project will turn into something. Whoever buys late pays for the confirmation that others were already convinced.

I didn't invent this. Every stock ticks this way, every sneaker drop, every artist's career. I'm just writing it down openly instead of letting it vanish behind gallery doors.

Honesty as conceptual art

In most galleries you don't even get to see the price. It's listed "on request." Price tags lie face down. That's not an oversight — it's method. Art isn't supposed to feel like business, it's supposed to feel like a truth only the initiated grasp.

I find that dishonest. And I say it as someone who sells art himself.

A fair price isn't one nobody discusses. A fair price is one anybody can see.

That's why on i-laugh-you you always see two numbers: what a piece costs right now — and where the curve is heading in the coming weeks. You buy today or you wait. You believe in the project or you don't. No haggling, no back-room prices. The price is the price.

What manufactured scarcity really is

"Limited edition" sounds like a law of nature. Like something that became scarce on its own. It isn't. Every limited edition is a desk decision. Someone said: "I'll print 100, not 10,000." The number was chosen to feel scarce while still bringing in enough revenue.

24,236 is an absurdly high number for an art print. It also happens to be the population of the Swiss municipality I live in. I picked it on purpose so that it would feel arbitrary — because it is arbitrary. So nobody can think I optimized it in Excel. I did not optimize it. I took it. There's a difference.

The point is: scarcity in art is always made. Without exception. The only question is whether the artist is honest enough to say so out loud.

Rembrandt did it too (and he knew it)

Amsterdam, 17th century. Rembrandt van Rijn paints oil portraits for wealthy merchants and at the same time etches portraits for bourgeois families. A painting goes to a single collector at top price. An etching he prints a hundred times over and sells for a fraction of that.

Both are Rembrandt. Both bear his signature. The market still values them completely differently — because the production method generates two different scarcities.

That's exactly how the art market still works today, just much more hidden. An NFT. A print. An original. Each format has its own price register. i-laugh-you stands squarely in that tradition: a modern etching, digitally numbered, with a price that moves like a real market. Rembrandt would have had a blast with it. He reworked his plates several times anyway to create new "states" — pure price manipulation, except he never called it that. I do.

Yes, this text is also marketing

At this point any other art blog would pretend it's all about the pure idea. I won't.

This text is also advertising. It's written for Google. It's packed with terms like art and capitalism, manufactured scarcity and dynamic pricing — so that the people googling those words end up here. I want to sell pieces. I have rent to pay. That's no secret, that's my everyday life.

The difference between me and the others: I'm telling you. I'm not hiding behind a gallery facade. The project is the critique, and the critique is the project. When you buy a piece, you're not just agreeing to an idea — you're agreeing to a method: transparency over mystification, arbitrariness placed openly on the table rather than hidden under it.

Whoever buys a piece casts a vote — one way or the other. On a market that has long since dragged you in, there's no neutral seat left.

What you actually own

A real, physical art print. On museum paper, framed in solid wood, shipped via Printful to the U.S., Canada, the U.K., the E.U. — wherever you want. A number between 1 and 24,236. A certificate stating exactly which slice of the original painting your fragment shows — coordinate by coordinate.

And a piece of a story. Whoever buys early shapes the curve for everyone who comes after. Whoever buys later gets the confirmation thrown in that the project actually works.

That's not neutral. It's not evil either. It's exactly how every art market functions — only I'm telling you up front.

Why 77 and why 777?

Because some numbers just sound right. $77 is affordable — a nice dinner for two at a good restaurant. $777 is a statement — a price you treat yourself to consciously. A whole world lies between those two values.

I could have picked 50 and 500. But 77 and 777 sound like lucky numbers, and in the end art is always a little superstition. You buy a picture because you hope it does something — for the room, for the mood, for your daily life, sometimes for the soul.

I don't deny it. I'm just saying: this belief has a price. And I'm printing it openly on the label instead of hiding it.

To close

You don't have to buy a piece for this project to work. You're allowed to just watch. Watch the curve bend. Watch real people make real decisions with real money. That's art too. Maybe the most honest kind around right now.

If you want to know what that actually feels like: here's the canvas. Click a fragment. Look at the current price. Read the certificate. Then decide — calmly, deliberately. That's all I'm asking.

And if you want to know how I ended up here in the first place: about the project. The whole story is there.
